At p=5 two numbers are joined when their difference is a nonzero square, 1 or 4, which gives a five-cycle. At p=3 and p=7, where -1 is not a square, the graph is directed: each pair gets exactly one arc, from x to x plus a nonzero square, making a tournament, a directed triangle at p=3 and 21 arcs at p=7." width="100%"} Creates `p` nodes `0, 1, ..., p - 1` and joins `x` to `x + s mod p` for every nonzero square `s` modulo `p` (the quadratic residues, of which a prime has `(p - 1) / 2`). When `p = 1 mod 4`, `-1` is a square, so the relation is symmetric and the Paley graph is an undirected, `(p - 1) / 2`-regular, strongly regular graph that is isomorphic to its own complement; Paley graphs are standard examples of pseudo-random graphs with excellent expansion. When `p = 3 mod 4`, exactly one of `x - y` and `y - x` is a square, and the directed version is the Paley tournament. In a directed graph every relation `x -> x + s` becomes an edge, as in NetworkX's `paley_graph()` (which returns a directed graph): for `p = 1 mod 4` each pair is joined in both directions. In an undirected graph each related pair gets a single edge, from the earlier-created node to the later one, so `p = 3 mod 4` gives a complete graph. `p` is not checked for primality. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Paley graphs are useful for: - strongly regular and self-complementary examples, with known spectra - pseudo-random graphs that behave like `G(p, 1/2)` but are fully deterministic - Paley tournaments, which are standard examples in tournament theory and Ramsey theory ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes, normally a prime. Must be non-negative. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `p=` is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The Paley graph of 13 is 6-regular and isomorphic to its own complement: ::: {#c09ece4c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_paley_graph(p=13) graph.count_edges(), set(graph.degrees(return_dict=True).values()), graph.is_isomorphic(graph.complement()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (39, {6}, True) ``` ::: ::: The Paley graph of 5 is the 5-cycle: ::: {#d7664c71 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} pentagon = ec.Graph().add_paley_graph(p=5) pentagon.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: For `p = 7` the directed version is a tournament: all `7 * 6 / 2 = 21` pairs are joined exactly once, and every node beats three others: ::: {#507e5768 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} tournament = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_paley_graph(p=7) tournament.count_edges(), [len(tournament.get_neighbors(v)) for v in tournament.get_node_ids()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (21, [3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3]) ``` ::: :::
